options.title: Standardized care in modern healthcare
options.preview: Analyzing digital check-in kiosks and tightly timed doctor visits revealed how hospitals adopt fast-food efficiency at the expense of individualized attention.

utilitarianism.definition: Utilitarianism is an ethical theory suggesting actions are right if they promote the greatest happiness for the greatest number, famously associated with Jeremy Bentham.

options.title: Compromising with friends and high school
options.preview: Choosing a restaurant to satisfy different friends and watching peers laugh at high school bullying prompted reflections on whether group happiness justifies harm.

options.title: First generation student and public policy
options.preview: Growing up around economic exploitation led to questioning whether viewing people as statistical numbers to maximize general welfare ignores personal dignity.

options.title: Allocating time and evaluating utility
options.preview: Prioritizing helping a struggling teammate over polishing a presentation prompted an evaluation of rule utilitarianism and individual rights.

commodity fetishism.definition: Karl Marx defined commodity fetishism as the perception of social relationships involved in production as economic relationships among money and commodities exchanged in market trade.

options.title: Buying goods without seeing labor
options.preview: Reflecting on consumer habits showed how purchasing everyday products hides the difficult labor and corporate exploitation behind them.

options.title: Childhood trends and popular headbands
options.preview: Conforming to a elementary school fashion trend meant begging for the exact same headband that every other girl wore.

options.title: Coffee culture and modern consumerism
options.preview: Analyzing Starbucks showed how consumers attach social prestige to drinks while ignoring the underlying chain production process.

options.title: Mall shopping for brand names
options.preview: Shoppers routinely prioritize expensive name brands at the mall over cheaper alternatives to acquire perceived social value.

options.title: Marketing gadgets and social status
options.preview: Examining consumer purchases of electronics illustrated how corporate marketing convinces people that products carry inherent social standing.

impression management.definition: Impression management is the process by which individuals attempt to control the impressions others form of them, as theorized by Erving Goffman.

systemic racism.definition: Systemic racism is institutional and cultural patterns that result in racial inequalities, formalized by sociologists like Joe Feagin.

options.title: Adoption and interracial family life
options.preview: Living alongside adopted Black siblings revealed sharp contrasts in how police and neighbors treated family members based on skin color.

options.title: Restaurant hiring and job channeling
options.preview: Working as a restaurant hostess exposed how Black staff were kept in the kitchen and excluded from customer facing server jobs.

options.title: Safety talks and school experiences
options.preview: Learning early childhood rules for interacting with police officers contrasted sharply with the experiences of white peers in school and ballet.

options.title: Donut shop job application
options.preview: Watching a qualified Black friend get passed over for a job at a local shop highlighted unearned white advantages.

options.title: Moving to a white university
options.preview: Leaving a diverse military community to attend a predominantly white college exposed institutional disparities and racial biases.

cohabitation.definition: Cohabitation is the practice of unmarried partners living together in a romantic relationship, often as a precursor or alternative to marriage.

options.title: Military support and future marriage
options.preview: Growing up with unmarried teenage parents led to discussions with a military boyfriend about living together and moving toward marriage.

options.title: Changing attitudes toward marriage commitment
options.preview: Watching a mother remain unmarried after divorce prompted reflections on why couples choose long-term cohabitation over legal marriage.

options.title: Cohabitation norms before marriage
options.preview: Examining changing cultural patterns led to questions about why couples live together before deciding on marriage.

options.title: College relationships and cohabitation trends
options.preview: Observing college peers choose to live together prompted analysis of how cohabitation serves as a stepping stone to marriage.

social solidarity.definition: Emile Durkheim defined social solidarity as the ties that bind a society together, categorized into mechanical and organic forms.

options.title: Military veteran culture in college
options.preview: Trained military reactions during civilian classes showed how wartime symbols and rituals forge deep bonds among veterans.

options.title: Preparing for a Bar Mitzvah
options.preview: Months of Hebrew lessons, volunteer piano performances, and temple rituals built a shared sense of community membership.

options.title: Questioning family religious traditions
options.preview: Doubts about church beliefs caused friction with a religious family that depended on shared faith for unity.

options.title: Growing up in a church community
options.preview: Attending interfaith events with a minister parent revealed how religious groups bond internally while dividing from outsiders.

backstage.definition: Erving Goffman defined the backstage as a place where individuals can relax and step out of character from their social performances.

options.title: Hiding family illness at school
options.preview: Masking personal fear and grief at school after a father's cancer diagnosis showed the exhaustion of keeping emotions behind closed doors.

options.title: Hiding depression while socializing
options.preview: Forcing a cheerful attitude during a night of bowling with friends contrasted sharply with feelings of severe depression experienced alone.

options.title: Conforming at a religious high school
options.preview: Faking devout religious participation during weekly chapel services required mentally preparing before school and dropping the act in private.

options.title: Balancing family and team roles
options.preview: Reflecting on behavioral changes between softball teams, college classrooms, and home life highlighted how backstage preparation shapes public roles.

options.title: Changing study habits in class
options.preview: Switching from a laptop to a paper notebook to match classmates during a lecture showed the contrast with studying alone in a dorm.

other.definition: The Other is any group or individual defined by the dominant group as fundamentally different or alien, a concept expanded by Simone de Beauvoir and Edward Said.

options.title: High school weightlifting as the only girl
options.preview: Enrolling in a high school weight training class led to isolation and hostile remarks from male peers and a substitute teacher.

options.title: Applying for manual labor jobs
options.preview: Applying for warehouse and shop positions resulted in male employers questioning physical capability and steering work toward the front counter.

options.title: Fraternity party door rejection
options.preview: Attending a fraternity party led to being evaluated by male hosts at the door while a friend was turned away.

options.title: Dynamics within a male friend group
options.preview: Hanging out as the only woman in a male friend group led to feeling objectified and excluded from equal consideration.

options.title: Coaching a youth soccer team
options.preview: Coaching youth soccer independently brought skeptical reactions from parents who questioned whether a woman could provide proper athletic instruction.
